topic: The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem: Finding Order in Chaos
target_audience: Undergraduate students in introductory statistics or data science

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of a Population vs. Sample
lecture_lines: A population represents every individual in a group.
A sample is just a small portion of them.
We describe groups using means and standard deviations.
animations: Draw a large cluster of diverse colored dots (#FFFFFF) representing 'Population'.
Circle a small subset of dots (#58C4DD) and label 'Sample'.
Transform the cluster into a jagged, bimodal distribution curve (#FFFF00).

sections.title: The Sampling Experiment: Taking Averages
lecture_lines: Stat-Bot selects five random members from our population.
We calculate the average value for this small sample.
This average becomes a single point in our bin.
We repeat this sampling process hundreds of times.
The resulting collection is the Sampling Distribution of the Mean.
animations: Animate a 'Stat-Bot' figure selecting 5 random shapes (#FF8080).
Calculate their average and display it as a dot (#FF8080).
Drop many dots into a bin to form a histogram (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: The Transformation: Emergence of the Bell Curve
lecture_lines: Observe how the population's starting shape is extremely jagged.
But the collection of sample averages forms a pattern.
It settles into a smooth, symmetric bell-shaped curve.
The same shape appears regardless of the starting distribution.
This transformation is the heart of the Central Limit Theorem.
animations: Show the bin from section 2 rapidly filling with dots (#FF8080).
Highlight a pattern emerging from the dense dot cluster (#FFFFFF).
Draw a vertical line through the center labeled 'μ' (#FFFF00).
Overlay a glowing Bell Curve outline (#00FF00) onto the histogram.
Flash the Bell Curve and text 'Central Limit Theorem' (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: The Law of Large Numbers (Sample Size n)
lecture_lines: Larger sample sizes create narrower and taller curves.
The spread is determined by the Standard Error formula.
Every curve centers exactly at the true population mean.
animations: Display a wide, short curve (n=2, #FFDAB9) on the left.
Highlight the wide base of the curve with arrows (#FFFFFF).
Display a narrow, tall curve (n=50, #87CEFA) on the right.
Shrink the width of the tall curve to show precision (#00FF00).
Display the formula 'SE = σ / √n' (#FFFF00) in center.

sections.title: Mathematical Definition & Key Properties
lecture_lines: Mathematically, the sample mean follows a Normal distribution.
Its center is exactly the population mean, mu.
The spread is the standard deviation divided by sqrt(n).
We write this as N(mu, sigma squared over n).
This holds true if the sample size is large enough.
animations: Display the CLT formula 'x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n)' (#FFFF00).
Highlight 'μ' and align it with the curve's peak (#00FF00).
Highlight 'σ²/n' and show it controlling curve width (#58C4DD).
Animate 'N' expanding into 'Normal Distribution' text (#FFFFFF).
Show 'n → ∞' as the curve becomes perfectly smooth (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: Application: Why It Matters in the Real World
lecture_lines: The CLT allows predictions without knowing the population shape.
It provides confidence for polling and scientific research.
Order emerges from chaos through the power of averages.
animations: Show a jagged distribution morphing into a smooth curve (#FFFFFF).
Display icons representing a poll and a medical trial (#87CEFA).
Fade in final text: 'Order from Chaos' (#FFFF00).
